question.text:
You are assessing the risk profiles of two investment portfolios: Portfolio X: Beta = 1.2, Standard Deviation = 15%. Portfolio Y: Beta = 0.8, Standard Deviation = 12%.
Using standard deviation as the measure of total volatility, which portfolio has the LOWER volatility?

answer.text: Both portfolios have the same volatility
Cannot determine from the given data

explanation.text: The Logic: Standard deviation captures total volatility (NISM-Series-XXI-A workbook, p.147). Portfolio X has standard deviation of 15% and Portfolio Y has 12%, so Portfolio Y is the lower-volatility portfolio. The stem now asks the direction explicitly (LOWER), so Portfolio Y is the unique answer. The Trap: Picking Portfolio X would be correct if the question asked for the HIGHER-volatility portfolio — which is exactly what made the original stem ambiguous, because it just said "rank the portfolios based on volatility" without specifying direction. "Same volatility" ignores the 3-percentage-point gap. "Cannot determine" wrongly claims beta is required — standard deviation alone captures total volatility per p.147. Note: The original stem ("Rank the portfolios based on volatility") did not specify low-to-high vs high-to-low and offered single-portfolio answer choices, so either Portfolio X (highest) or Portfolio Y (lowest) could be defended. The stem has been tightened to ask explicitly for the LOWER-volatility portfolio, making Portfolio Y the unique answer.
